claims.claim: Every connected cograph other than a singleton or a graph with exactly one universal vertex is equivalent to the zero game.
claims.evidence: A connected cograph's canonical root is a join. Two universal vertices form a pairing dominating set. If there is no universal vertex, every root-join block has at least two vertices; choosing two vertices from each of two blocks gives disjoint pairs whose common closed neighborhoods cover the whole graph. Remark 9 then gives contextual equivalence to zero.
claims.witness: For pairs (a,b) in one join block and (c,d) in another, N[a]∩N[b] contains every vertex outside the first block, while N[c]∩N[d] contains the entire first block.
claims.search_method: Direct cotree case analysis and exhaustive exact minimax over every labeled cograph on at most six vertices.

claims.claim: SHVG on cographs is polynomially equivalent to an explicit open-or-delete scoring game on rooted forests.
claims.evidence: The universal-vertex transposition works for either player in every disjoint context. Breaker ownership of the universal vertex makes the component a zero position. After Maker owns it, preassigning a twin pair in C-u to opposite players spoils the universal vertex and makes every remaining happiness condition identical to C-u. Conversely, K2 ballast yields a unique universal vertex and preserves the child forest. Degenerate zero projects have equal scores zero and may be discarded by Theorem 6.
claims.witness: Swapping a proposed move x with the universal vertex u either leaves the final coloring unchanged on {u,x}, or compares a coloring where Breaker owns u and the component scores zero against a nonnegative component score. The inverse construction uses one new universal vertex and a disjoint zero K2 per internal node, totaling L+3I vertices.
claims.search_method: Contextual strategy-transposition proof, twin-position comparison, constructive inverse reduction, and exhaustive labeled-cograph minimax checks.

claims.claim: Both starting-player variants on arbitrary reduced forests are threshold-preservingly reducible with linear node blowup to Maker-first play on a single rooted tree; consequently SHVG on all cographs is polynomially equivalent to Maker-first SHVG on connected cographs.
claims.evidence: S1 has both scores zero, so wrapping F+S1 under a new root converts Maker-first play into B(F). For Maker-first F with L prizes, wrapping F+S_{2L+2} converts the query into B(F+S_{2L+2}). Breaker can obtain M(F) by deleting the star; every other deletion lets Maker open it, after which Theorem 5 gives Breaker-first value at least floor((2L+2)/2)=L+1>M(F). Both constructions add O(L) nodes and preserve the exact threshold.
claims.search_method: Direct minimax inequalities, boundary-case analysis, and exhaustive exact tests on 165 small forests.

claims.claim: The cograph game is linear-time solvable when every tree in the reduced forest has outdegree at most two.
claims.evidence: Inductively every binary subtree is equivalent to zero Z or one prize A. An internal root with zero or one A-type child has equal starting scores zero and hence is Z. With two A-type children, the exposed sum A+A is the constant game 1, so the root is {1|0}=A. Zero children may be omitted contextually. A forest with z surviving A-types therefore has scores ceil(z/2) and floor(z/2), computable by one bottom-up pass.
claims.witness: The complete transition table by number of A-type children is 0→Z, 1→Z, and 2→A.
claims.search_method: Structural induction using Theorem 6, followed by exhaustive exact checks of 398 binary rooted trees and 2,380 small binary forests.

claims.claim: Reduced forests of height one—equivalently, disjoint unions of stars and isolated vertices after zero components are removed—admit an O(n^2) exact algorithm.
claims.evidence: The unrestricted recurrence considers an exposed leaf and every remaining star. A simultaneous induction on remaining nodes proves star-size monotonicity and the exchange inequality V_X(S∪{j},l+k)≥V_X(S∪{k},l+j) for j≤k: exposed-leaf moves, moves in S, and moves at the distinguished stars match after one move, while the distinguished-star case uses monotonicity in exposed leaves. Thus opening or deleting a largest star is optimal. The resulting two-parameter recurrence has O(rK)⊆O(n^2) states.
claims.witness: M(i,l)=max(1+B(i,l-1),B(i-1,l+k_i)) and B(i,l)=min(M(i,l-1),M(i-1,l)), with M(0,l)=ceil(l/2) and B(0,l)=floor(l/2).
claims.search_method: Proof of the exchange induction plus exact comparison with unrestricted minimax for every height-one state through 32 total nodes, covering 43,820 states.

claims.claim: The pair of standalone scores (Ms,Bs) is insufficient as a cotree dynamic-programming state.
claims.evidence: Direct minimax gives both P3 and K1,3 standalone scores (1,0), while their behavior in disjoint sums differs: P3+P3 has (1,1), but P3+K1,3 has (2,1). Hence any compositional state retaining only the two standalone scores identifies inequivalent components.
claims.witness: P3 and K1,3 are the rooted projects S2 and S3; the exact score pairs of S2+S2 and S2+S3 are respectively (1,1) and (2,1).
claims.search_method: Direct exact minimax in both the original graph game and the rooted-forest recurrence.

claims.claim: For every integer r≥1, two height-two rooted projects have the same 4r+2 nodes, 4r prize leaves, height, outdegree multiset, and standalone scores (r,0), yet adjoining one prize leaf gives scores (r,1) and (r+1,1), respectively.
claims.evidence: For k≥2, exact minimax gives B(lA+S_k)=ceil(l/2): deleting S_k attains that value, while deleting an exposed leaf lets Maker open S_k and yields at least floor((l-1+k)/2)≥ceil(l/2). Substitution into X_r=R((2r-1)A+S_{2r+1}) and Y_r=R(2rA+S_{2r}) proves all score formulas. Direct counting gives the common node, leaf, height, and outdegree data.
claims.witness: Both projects have outdegrees {2r,2r+1} plus 4r zeros. Their standalone scores are (r,0), while A+X_r has (r,1) and A+Y_r has (r+1,1).
claims.search_method: Symbolic integer inequalities and exact minimax checks for r=1 through r=7, including all cited auxiliary formulas.

claims.claim: Breaker's strict preference between two rooted-project types can reverse with the surrounding forest, so no rule whose choice between those roots depends only on their individual types can always prescribe an optimal deletion.
claims.evidence: With U=S4 and V=R(2A+U), exact recurrence gives M(U)=2, M(V)=1, M(2U)=2, and M(U+V)=3. Thus in U+V, deleting U leaves value 1 whereas deleting V leaves 2, making U uniquely optimal. In U+U+V, deleting U leaves 3 whereas deleting V leaves 2, making V uniquely optimal. The strict reversal rules out a context-independent comparison of the two types.
claims.witness: Breaker successor values are (delete U, delete V)=(1,2) in U+V and (3,2) in U+U+V.
claims.search_method: Direct recurrence evaluation and independent exact minimax reproduction of every auxiliary value.

target_evidence: The source target requires either a polynomial-time algorithm or a matching hardness theorem for all cographs. The draft supplies correct structural reductions, two polynomial subcases, and genuine obstructions to simple dynamic-programming states, but explicitly leaves arbitrary rooted trees unresolved. It therefore makes material partial progress without resolving the full target, matching its claimed PARTIAL status.
